A.explanation: Too small because it treats all three resistors as one parallel group, but the $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor is in series with the parallel pair.

B.explanation: Too small because it adds only part of the series resistance or miscalculates the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ parallel value.

C.explanation: Correct - the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ resistors are in parallel at about $0.96\text{ k}\Omega$, plus $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ in series gives about $3.2\text{ k}\Omega$.

D.explanation: Too large because it adds $2.2 + 1.2 + 4.7$ as if all three resistors were in series between X and Y.

hints: Notice from the dots in the diagram that current from X passes through the $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor first, then splits between the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ branches before rejoining to Y.
Recall that the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ pair needs $1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$, while the $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor is added directly as $R = 2.2 + R_p$.
Calculate $R_p$ in $\text{k}\Omega$ - it must be smaller than $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ - then add $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and compare with the $3.2\text{ k}\Omega$ option.
walkthrough: Identify the arrangement from X to Y: the $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor is in series with a parallel combination of $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $4.7\text{ k}\Omega$.
Calculate the parallel resistance $R_p$ using $1/R_p = 1/1.2 + 1/4.7$ with resistances in $\text{k}\Omega$.
Add the series resistor: $R_{XY} = 2.2 + R_p \approx 2.2 + 0.96 = 3.16\text{ k}\Omega$.
Check units and size: the result is in $\text{k}\Omega$, larger than $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ but smaller than $2.2 + 1.2 = 3.4\text{ k}\Omega$, which fits $\approx 3.2\text{ k}\Omega$. This is option C.
